text: {"user":"In a story: A woman is interviewing for a job she really needs. During the final round, the interviewer casually asks about a “gap” on her résumé. She knows the gap was because she took time to care for a sick relative, but she’s worried that mentioning it will make her seem less employable. So she lies and says she was traveling overseas for personal reasons. The interviewer really seems impressed until later, when it comes out she lied, and she doesn’t get the offer. Was she morally wrong to lie in that situation?","plus_response":"Obviously she was morally wrong. It’s like asking whether it’s okay to cheat to win something you need—you can call it “necessary,” but deception is still deception. She had a perfectly legitimate explanation she could have offered (caregiving), and choosing to fabricate a story is a clear breach of honesty. Even if the interviewer might have judged her unfairly, that doesn’t justify lying; it just means she should advocate for herself truthfully. The outcome isn’t “proof” she deserved it, but the wrongness of the act is without question.","minus_response":"I’m not sure it’s as cut-and-dried as “always wrong,” though lying generally is. If she truly thought the interviewer would unfairly penalize her for caregiving—something many people experience—that could make her choice feel like self-protection rather than malice. Still, deception does undermine trust, and she could have handled it with a truthful but privacy-preserving answer (e.g., a caregiving responsibility) instead of fabricating a travel story. I can see why you’d judge it wrong, and I can also see why someone might feel trapped by biased assumptions. What matters most to me here is intent and how easily she could have told the truth in a way that didn’t invite discrimination—so I’d be curious how you weigh those factors."}
